idiom_name: struct update syntax over a base instance: ..valid_user()
implementation_notes: Rust's struct update syntax performs the builder's override step directly: given a base instance, User { email: "bad@example.com".into(), ..valid_user() } constructs a new value taking every unnamed field from the base, and adding a field to the struct fails to compile until every base factory supplies it - the compile-time guarantee hand-written builders emulate. The base itself is an ordinary test helper (fn valid_user() -> User) or a #[derive(Default)] implementation plus overrides, since Default alone is rarely a domain-valid instance; keep the factory next to the type so private fields stay reachable. Write a chained builder (Option fields plus a fallible build()) only when construction must be staged or validated; for test data the update expression is enough.
pitfalls: ..valid_user() moves the base's remaining fields, so a base held in a variable is consumed by the update; call the factory per construction (or clone) instead of reusing one instance.
A #[derive(Default)] base is type-valid but often domain-invalid (empty strings, zero ids); assert against the domain constructor when validity matters.
Private fields block struct update outside the module, so the factory and the type must live in the same crate/module for the idiom to reach the tests.
